tldr: To smoothly connect independently acquired humanoid motion clips, the authors propose "STAMP," a framework that maps motions into a shared human motion space, predicts the optimal relative position, heading, and transition duration, and then generates intermediate transition motions using a generative model. Experiments on physical robots demonstrate stable motion transitions accompanied by natural stepping.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of STAMP. Individual robot motions are first retargeted to a human rig (skeletal model). An alignment model then scores and determines the relative position, heading, and transition duration for the following motion. Under these chosen boundary conditions, a human motion generative model produces a natural intermediate transition, which is retargeted back to the robot and used as a reference trajectory for training a tracking policy.
overview:
When enabling humanoid robots to perform diverse behaviors, techniques for tracking individual motion clips—such as punching or running—with high quality have advanced significantly. However, naturally connecting two independently created motions (motion transition) remains a challenging problem. Simple interpolation fails to account for foot switching or weight shifts, causing foot skating. On the other hand, directly applying generative models without well-defined boundary conditions—such as where to place the following motion, which direction it should face, and how many seconds the transition should take—leads to unnatural detours or unintended actions.

To solve this, the authors retarget robot motions into a shared human skeletal space and train an alignment model on continuous human motion data to evaluate what relative arrangement and timing allow for a smooth transition. Using this model to determine the optimal relative position, heading, and transition duration, the proposed "STAMP" framework generates intermediate motions with a human motion prior (motion inbetweening model) and maps them back to the robot—a "Robot-to-Human-to-Robot" approach.

In simulation and real-robot evaluations using two distinct humanoid robots, Unitree G1 and ROBOTIS K1, STAMP achieved higher tracking success rates and smoother joint motions than baselines. Furthermore, demonstrations on the physical robot validated dynamic transitions involving stepping into punches, as well as the execution of long-horizon multi-task sequences.
contributions: Proposed "STAMP," a "Robot-to-Human-to-Robot" framework that maps individual robot motions into a shared human motion space to leverage rich motion priors and generate transitions reusable across different robot embodiments.

Constructed a spatio-temporal alignment model that evaluates and ranks candidate relative positions, headings, and transition durations for the following motion using continuous human motion data and counterfactual arrangements.

Quantitatively demonstrated improvements in tracking success rates and jerk in Unitree G1 and ROBOTIS K1 simulations, and validated dynamic transitions with stepping and long-horizon sequence stitching on a physical ROBOTIS K1.

sections.heading: Why Is Connecting Robot Motions So Difficult?
sections.summary: Even if individual motion clips can be reproduced, smoothly executing independently created motions in sequence is non-trivial. Simple interpolation or poorly chosen boundary arrangements cause foot contact and balance to break down. This study proposes STAMP, which determines suitable boundary arrangements and transition timing in human motion space before inbetweening.
sections.details:
Recent advances in physics-simulation-based imitation learning allow humanoid robots to faithfully track dynamic motions. However, connecting independently acquired motion clips into a continuous sequence presents challenges distinct from tracking a single behavior.

When motions are prepared as separate clips, spatio-temporal information is missing: at what relative position and heading should the following motion begin relative to the preceding motion, and how many seconds should the transition take? Even if each motion looks natural on its own, connecting boundaries with an arbitrary relative configuration requires unnatural torso twisting or abrupt posture changes.

Returning to a neutral pose before starting the next motion is an option, but it completely disrupts the flow of movement. Meanwhile, directly interpolating between boundary poses using splines ignores the momentum of preceding and following motions, as well as support foot switching. For a humanoid, changing the support leg requires stepping and weight shifting; pure pose interpolation thus leads to foot skating or falling over.

On the other hand, recent generative motion inbetweening models can produce rich human motions. However, poorly arranged boundary positions or timings cause them to generate excessive locomotion or unintended turning. To address this, the authors propose "STAMP," which ranks candidate boundary configurations via human motion space, generates natural transitions, and retargets them back to the robot.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of Humanoid Control, Motion Inbetweening, and Retargeting
sections.summary: The authors summarize three lines of prior work—reinforcement-learning-based humanoid motion tracking, deep generative models for human motion inbetweening, and cross-embodiment motion retargeting—and explain how STAMP integrates them to overcome key transition challenges.
sections.details:
This work connects three primary research areas:

### II-A Humanoid Motion Tracking and Transitions
Imitation learning in physics simulation (such as DeepMimic and AMP) has enabled humanoids to track complex reference motions with high fidelity. For transitions between motions, methods connecting similar states via graphs (Switch), motion matching (Perceptive Humanoid Parkour), and multi-policy blending (RPG) have been explored. However, because these switch states mid-motion, they truncate or alter the original motion content. STAMP preserves the original input clips completely while generating a reference trajectory that smoothly connects the end of one clip to the start of the next.

### II-B Human Motion Inbetweening
Techniques for generating intermediate frames given past and future contexts have advanced rapidly with diffusion models. In robotics, motion inbetweening has also been applied to control the Unitree G1 (MotionBricks). However, existing models assume boundary conditions cropped from a single continuous capture—where natural relative positions and time deltas are already known. To connect independent clips, a mechanism to determine boundary placement and transition duration before running the generative model is essential.

### II-C Human-Robot Motion Retargeting
Retargeting techniques that map human motion to robot kinematic limits and link lengths range from geometric approaches to learning-based methods. This work extends the bidirectional retargeting method CoRe, projecting robot-specific motions into human space to generate transitions and returning them to the robot—treating human motion space as a shared common domain.

sections.heading: Formulating Smooth Transitions Between Independent Motions
sections.summary: Given two independent robot motion clips—a preceding motion and a following motion—this section outlines the formulation for generating a physically trackable transition sequence that connects them into a single continuous sequence without altering the original clips.
sections.details:
Consider a robot $R$ given two independently acquired clips: a preceding motion $\mathcal{M}_{P}^{R}$ ($T_{P}$ frames) and a following motion $\mathcal{M}_{F}^{R}$ ($T_{F}$ frames). Each frame contains root pose and joint angle information.

Because these motions were captured separately, the initial planar position, heading, and time interval of the following motion relative to the end of the preceding motion are undefined. The goal is to generate a transition motion $\mathcal{T}_{P\rightarrow F}^{R}$ that bridges the end of the preceding motion to the start of the following motion without modifying the content or order of the original clips, assembling them into a single sequence.

The generated transition must provide smooth body motion and foot support transitions that a robot tracking policy can physically follow, without unnecessary retreats to a neutral pose or excessive turning.

sections.heading: STAMP: Selecting Optimal Configurations via Human Space for Inbetweening
sections.summary: STAMP retargets robot motions to a human rig, determines the following motion's optimal position, heading, and duration using a spatio-temporal alignment model, generates a transition with a diffusion model, and maps it back to the robot for policy training.
sections.details:
At the core of STAMP is a pipeline that retargets robot motions to a human skeleton (SOMA) to absorb embodiment differences, performs alignment and inbetweening in human space, and retargets the sequence back to the robot.

### IV-A Spatio-Temporal Motion Alignment
An alignment candidate $\mathbf{c} = (\Delta\mathbf{p}_{c}, \Delta\psi_{c}, \tau_{c})$ is defined by the following motion's initial planar position $\Delta\mathbf{p}_{c}$, yaw heading $\Delta\psi_{c}$, and transition duration $\tau_{c}$, all relative to the root frame at the end of the preceding motion. The entire following motion is rigidly transformed by this offset.

The alignment model $E_{\phi}$ takes kinematic features (root, joint positions, velocities, foot contact states, etc.) from the last $K$ frames of the preceding motion and the first $K$ frames of the transformed following motion to predict a scalar "transition cost" reflecting transition naturalness. The model processes past and future contexts via two Transformer encoders, feeding their difference, product, and transition duration into an MLP to output the cost.

To train this model, counterfactual samples with altered spatial placements and temporal scaling are generated alongside continuous transitions from human motion data. The model is trained using a combination of KL divergence against a preference distribution and regression loss targeting a kinematic cost $E_{\mathrm{tgt}}$, which penalizes joint acceleration, jerk, foot dynamics, floor skating, and unnatural idling.

### IV-B Particle-Based Inference
During inference, 388 fixed candidate particles are evaluated in parallel: 4 $\times$ 4 planar position offsets, 6 headings, 4 durations (0.5s, 1.0s, 1.5s, 2.0s), plus an origin candidate. Without generating full intermediate motions, the candidate $\mathbf{c}^*$ with the lowest predicted cost is instantly selected.

### IV-C Human Motion Inbetweening
Under the selected placement and duration, a diffusion model (a two-stage Transformer based on Kimodo) generates the intermediate frames. The first stage generates the 3D root trajectory and heading, while the second stage denoises full-body joint motion conditioned on the root trajectory and boundary contexts.

### IV-D Bidirectional Motion Retargeting
When mapping from robot to human (Robot-to-Human), the process scales skeletal proportions while preserving foot contact sequences and orientations. After transition generation, the sequence is mapped back from human to robot (Human-to-Robot) as a single unified sequence, yielding reference motions that respect the robot's joint limits and link proportions.

Middle: The alignment model scores and selects the optimal placement and duration from candidate particles, followed by motion inbetweening. Bottom: The completed sequence is retargeted back to the robot.

sections.heading: Simulations and Real-Robot Experiments: High Success Rates and Natural Stepping
sections.summary: Using Unitree G1 and ROBOTIS K1, tracking performance was evaluated across 18 motion pairs spanning boxing and inspection tasks. STAMP achieved higher success rates and smoother joint motions than baselines, demonstrating natural stepping transitions and long continuous sequences on the physical robot.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup
The authors prepared 18 motion pairs across three domains: boxing (8 pairs), industrial inspection (5 pairs), and security/traffic control (5 pairs). Baselines included quintic polynomial root/heading interpolation, "Kimodo †" (using the same diffusion inbetweening model but keeping boundary placement at the origin), and the prior method "MotionBricks" (evaluated on G1). Tracking policies were trained and evaluated for each robot using reinforcement learning (BeyondMimic) based on the generated reference motions.

### V-C Pairwise Motion Transition Tracking Results
Evaluation was conducted over 1,024 trials per pair (18,432 trials in total). In tracking success rate (the percentage of trials reaching the end within error thresholds), STAMP achieved 80.69% on Unitree G1 and 87.52% on ROBOTIS K1, outperforming all baselines. It also achieved the lowest body velocity error ($E_{\mathrm{vel}}$) and joint acceleration. The substantial improvement over Kimodo †—which shares the same generative backbone—confirms the critical importance of optimizing spatio-temporal boundary placement prior to generation.

### V-D Ablation on Alignment Ranking
Comparing candidates ranked 1st (Rank 1) versus 100th (Rank 100) by the alignment model revealed that Rank 1 achieved a 15.62 percentage point higher success rate on ROBOTIS K1 and a 9.36 point higher rate on G1, alongside reduced joint acceleration. This confirms that the learned cost strongly correlates with physical tracking feasibility.

### V-E Physical Robot Validation (ROBOTIS K1)
In physical experiments transitioning from "run" to "punch," the interpolation baseline caused the robot to abruptly decelerate and slip at the end of the run. In contrast, STAMP placed the punch forward, allowing the robot to take natural forward steps during the transition before throwing the punch (Figure F2). Motor current RMS measurements showed lower load and trial-to-trial variance in the second half of the transition (Figure F3). Furthermore, STAMP successfully enabled the physical robot to execute a stable, long-horizon sequence stitching four traffic-directing motions (Figure F4).

captions.F2: Transition from "run" to "punch" on the physical ROBOTIS K1 (progressing right to left). Top: The interpolation baseline abruptly halts and slips due to lack of forward space. Bottom: STAMP places the following motion forward, generating natural stepping forward during the transition.
captions.F3: Motor current RMS response across all 23 actuators during the transition from "look around" to "stop gesture" on ROBOTIS K1. Showing mean and standard deviation over 5 trials, STAMP (blue) exhibits lower average current and trial-to-trial variation in the second half of the transition compared to interpolation (red).
captions.F4: Execution of a long-horizon sequence connecting four traffic gestures on the physical ROBOTIS K1. Repeatedly applying STAMP allows flexible synthesis of continuous, stable behaviors from multiple independent motion clips.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: STAMP successfully connects independently acquired humanoid motions by selecting appropriate spatio-temporal boundary conditions in human motion space and interpolating with a generative model. Its primary strength lies in reusing transition knowledge across diverse robot embodiments.
sections.details:
This paper presented STAMP, a framework for naturally connecting independently acquired humanoid motion clips.

The core of STAMP combines an alignment model that evaluates the relative position, heading, and duration of the following motion with a generative model that produces natural human transitions. Operating within a shared human motion space allows transition knowledge to be shared and reused across diverse humanoid embodiments without being tightly bound to a specific robot's kinematics.

Experiments confirmed that STAMP outperformed baselines in tracking success rates on both Unitree G1 and ROBOTIS K1, while physical robot demonstrations validated smooth stepping transitions and long-horizon sequence execution without failure.

takeaways: Before running a motion inbetweening model, properly deciding the relative position, heading, and duration of the target motion largely dictates the success of physical tracking.

Adopting a "Robot-to-Human-to-Robot" design that maps robot motions to a shared human skeleton allows rich human motion data and pre-trained generative models to be reused across different embodiments.
In humanoid transitions, deliberately providing space and time to take steps—rather than forcing static interpolation—effectively prevents foot skating and tipping caused by abrupt stops.
limitations: Because the alignment model evaluates kinematic costs, it does not directly model joint limit constraints during retargeting or actual robot dynamics (such as torque limits).

A tracking policy must be trained for each generated sequence, incurring computational overhead that currently prevents zero-shot immediate execution of arbitrary sequences (noted by the authors as future work on policy unification).
